definition: A spot on the lung, smaller than 3 centimeters (or less than 30 millimeters), that looks different from surrounding normal lung tissue on imaging tests.
symptoms: Small lung nodules rarely cause symptoms; Chest pain; Shortness of breath (dyspnea) or wheezing; Chronic cough or coughing up blood; Fatigue; Hoarseness; Loss of appetite and unexplained weight loss; Recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia
causes: Infections; Inhaled particles; Inflammatory conditions; Scarring (fibrosis); Cancer
diagnosis: Chest X-rays; CT scan (including active surveillance every 6 to 12 months); PET scan; Blood tests (to look for infections or other causes); Sputum tests (to look for infections or other causes); Tissue sample (biopsy) including Bronchoscopy, Thoracoscopy, Video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS), and Needle biopsy; Removing the entire nodule
treatments: Small, noncancerous lung nodules usually don't require treatment; Active surveillance with additional imaging in 6 to 12 months; Medications for infection-caused nodules (antibiotics or antifungal medications); Surgery (if the nodule grows, causes symptoms, or blocks an airway)
complications: Small possibility of being cancerous; Pressing against or blocking an airway (rare for noncancerous nodules)
outlook: Most lung nodules are benign (not cancerous); Benign nodules will usually stay the same size or go away on their own; Nodules staying the same size during a two-year surveillance period are unlikely to be cancer; Nodules smaller than 0.6 cm and those with smooth edges are less likely to be cancerous; Nodules <5 mm have a <1% chance of being cancerous; Nodules 5 mm to 10 mm have up to a 28% chance of being cancerous; Nodules >2 cm (approaching lung mass size) have a 64% to 82% chance of malignancy; Nodules can sometimes begin to grow
life_expectancy: Most pulmonary nodules aren't harmful and don't affect survival; If cancerous, survival rate depends on cancer type and stage
prevention: Not much can be done to prevent benign nodules; Quitting smoking to keep lungs healthy
living_with: Follow up with healthcare provider for additional tests or surveillance; Monitor for symptoms like shortness of breath or chronic cough; Seek ER/911 for chest pain, difficulty breathing, or coughing up blood
risk_factors: Smoking or past history of smoking; Age older than 65; Family history or personal history of cancer; Past radiation therapy to the chest; Exposure to asbestos, radon, or secondhand smoke

complications: Some benign causes can cause serious health complications; Malignancy / cancer spread

definition: Enlarged heart; a heart that's bigger than what's typical. The heart may be unusually thick or dilated (stretched), short-term or permanent, and can affect the whole heart or just parts of it.

diagnosis: Discussing symptoms, biological family health history, and physical activity; Physical exam (listening with stethoscope for heart murmur, checking for signs of heart failure like leg swelling, crackles in lungs, engorged neck veins); Chest X-ray; Cardiac CT scan; Echocardiogram; Electrocardiogram (EKG); Exercise stress test; Heart MRI; Genetic testing
treatments: Lifestyle changes (reduce salt intake, avoid tobacco use, eat heart-healthy foods, regular physical activity, stay at healthy weight, reduce alcohol intake, manage fluid intake); Antiarrhythmics; Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors; Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs); Anticoagulants; Beta-blockers; Diuretics (salt pills or water pills); Implanting a pacemaker; Placing an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD); Repairing or replacing a damaged heart valve; Placing a stent or performing coronary artery bypass surgery
complications: Blood clots (can lead to heart attack, stroke, or pulmonary embolism); Heart failure (if left side is enlarged/left ventricular hypertrophy or dilated); Heart murmur; Sudden cardiac death (from deadly abnormal heart rhythms)
outlook: Can be short-term or permanent depending on the cause; Can be serious or mild depending on the underlying condition; If caused by a short-term factor (like pregnancy or an infection), the heart returns to its usual size after treatment; If caused by a chronic condition, it usually won't go away and requires ongoing medication/treatment to manage symptoms; Some complications can be fatal; Many people effectively manage symptoms; Early treatment can stop the condition from getting worse; earlier care gives better chances for a good outcome

definition: A condition developing when scar tissue thickens the delicate lining around the lungs (the pleura).
symptoms: Often asymptomatic in early stages; Chest pain; Cough; Difficulty catching your breath; Difficulty or inability to take a deep breath; Fatigue; Fever; Pain when exhaling or inhaling; Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially after or during exertion; Breathlessness during physical activity

diagnosis: Chest X-ray; CT scan; Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); Physical examination (checking for physical symptoms, such as altered breathing sounds); Positron emission tomography (PET scan); Ultrasound; Biopsies; Respiratory function tests (analyzing diffusing capacity and testing lung volume)
treatments: Many cases do not require treatment; Treatment for the underlying cause; Pulmonary rehabilitation; Cessation of smoking; Exercising regularly; Improving diet and nutrition; Learning breathing strategies; Learning how to conserve energy; Pleurectomy and decortication (P/D) surgical procedure (in rare, serious cases); Regular respiratory function tests
complications: Limited lung function; Impaired breathing; Severe lung restriction (in rare cases)
outlook: Progressive disease; symptoms often become more severe over time; Not always serious; Long-term effects are fairly mild in most cases; Can be benign (typically will not impede normal lung functioning unless advanced); Cannot be cured, but treatment can help manage symptoms; Not documented to be fatal on its own; Prognosis may depend on underlying condition (like lung disease or mesothelioma)

definition: A progressive disease characterized by lung scarring, stiffness, and impaired healing from damage or inflammation.
symptoms: Shortness of breath, especially during or soon after exertion; Breathing in short, shallow spurts; Dry cough that doesn’t go away; Fatigue; Unexplained weight loss; Clubbed fingers; Bluish, gray or white skin around your lips, eyes or nails (cyanosis)

diagnosis: Listening to lungs; Pulmonary (lung) function tests; Ruling out other conditions that affect heart and lungs; Chest X-ray; High-resolution CT (HRCT) scan; Blood tests, including an arterial blood gas; Bronchoscopy; Biopsy; Echocardiogram
treatments: Antifibrotic medications (Nintedanib / OFEV®, pirfenidone / Esbriet®); Corticosteroids; Oxygen therapy; Pulmonary rehabilitation; Lung transplant; Clinical trials; Medications to treat underlying causes (like autoimmune disease) or conditions that make scarring worse (like GERD)
complications: Low oxygen in your blood (hypoxemia) and tissues (hypoxia); High blood pressure in your lungs (pulmonary hypertension); Collapsed lung; Lung infections; Respiratory failure; Heart failure
outlook: Permanent and usually gets progressively worse over time; Lung scarring is nearly always permanent (unless caused by a medication and caught early); Healthcare providers can't easily predict how it will progress; symptoms may get worse very slowly over years or lead to severe symptoms quickly over months
prevention: Avoiding substances that can harm your lungs (asbestos, metal dust, chemicals) and wearing a respirator mask if working with them; Avoiding things that can cause chronic allergic reactions (hay, grain, bird droppings, feathers, heating/cooling systems) and wearing a respirator mask if working with them; Not smoking or quitting smoking
living_with: Washing hands frequently, disinfecting surfaces, and avoiding crowded places; Getting recommended vaccinations (pneumonia, flu, RSV, COVID)

diagnosis: Physical exam (listening to heart and lungs with a stethoscope); Checking for increased or decreased heart rate or blood pressure; Checking for increased respiratory rate; Checking for abnormal heart sounds; Checking for crackling sounds or wheezing/whistling sounds in lungs; Checking for swelling of body; Checking for gray or bluish skin; Complete blood count (CBC); Blood chemistries; Pulse oximetry; Chest X-ray; Echocardiogram; Electrocardiogram (EKG); Cardiac catheterization
treatments: Oxygen delivered through prongs in your nose; Machines that blow air into your lungs through a mask on your face; Ventilators or respirators that blow in air through a tube inserted into your windpipe; Medications that cause you to urinate more and get rid of fluid; Medications that strengthen your heart; Antibiotics; Steroids
outlook: Can be life-threatening and requires immediate medical treatment; Survival rates depend on the cause of the condition and how quickly you receive treatment; Severe cases can be life-threatening if you don't receive treatment right away
prevention: Take medications as directed if you have a heart condition; Get routine vaccinations; See your healthcare provider regularly and if you have problems breathing; Eat a healthy diet low in salt; Don't smoke; Maintain a healthy weight; Talk to your provider if you're planning activities (such as mountain climbing) that can cause pulmonary edema

condition_name: High Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE) (Noncardiogenic Causes (Inflammation or Injury to Blood Vessels in Lungs))
definition: A noncardiogenic form of pulmonary edema occurring at high elevations due to reduced oxygen pressure.
symptoms: Tiredness; Weakness; Aches; Shortness of breath; Coughing; Chest tightness
causes: Being at high altitudes or rapidly going up (ascending) a mountain; Lower oxygen levels at higher altitudes; Pulmonary blood vessels constricting and becoming leaky

treatments: Descending (going down) immediately; Medical treatment
outlook: Medical emergency and can be life-threatening
